1	# User research — the four target segments
2	
3	## Key insights
4	
5	- Israel votes on 27 October 2026 — a fixed deadline, and the first Knesset to serve a full term since 1988
6	- Trust in Israeli media averages 46% and splits by channel, from Kan 11 at 60% down to Channel 14 at 35%
7	- 52% of Israelis get news through WhatsApp or Telegram — messaging is a primary news channel, not a side one
8	- The benchmark Israeli media survey covers only the Jewish public; the 2.1M Arab citizens were not measured
9	- Israel's professional fact-checking segment is one newsroom desk, so the field is a supplier, not a rival
10	- Israel fell to 112th in RSF's 2025 press-freedom index from 101st, and the cabinet cut off Haaretz's state ads
11	- Backfire effect failed to replicate: 10,000+ subjects, 52 issues, zero backfires — corrections do move beliefs
12	
13	## Who these segments actually are in Israel
14	
15	The four segments below were researched against the US and are kept as transferable background on how people respond to corrections and what practitioners need. This section is the Israeli reading of the same four, and it is where the sizes and the habits come from.
16	
17	**The public: online, messaged, and only half-trusting.** The Israel Democracy Institute's media survey (published 26 May 2024, led by Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler and Inna Orly Sapozhnikova) found 63% of respondents check news online daily, 59.5% use social media for news, 58% rely on television, **52% get news through WhatsApp or Telegram**, 36% radio and 16% print. Average trust in the media stood at 46%, split hard by outlet: Kan 11 at 60%, Channel 12 at 54%, Channel 13 at 46%, Channel 14 at 35%. 56% believe they can distinguish fake news from factual reporting, and about 70% believe they can separate news from commentary ([IDI: Media and Social Media Consumption, Trust, and Literacy](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/54235)). Two things follow. Messaging apps are a first-class news channel here in a way they are not in the US data above, so a shareable per-statement link matters more than a destination site. And the trust split runs by *channel*, not only by party — which is the Israeli form of the partisan-audience problem the US section describes.
18	
19	**A fifth of the country is outside the survey and outside the language.** The IDI survey covered the Jewish population only; a companion survey of Arab citizens' habits was planned separately. Arab citizens are 2.147 million people, 21.1% of the population ([CBS figures as reported](https://israel.com/public/israel-starts-2026-with-more-than-10-million-people/)). A Hebrew-only product does not serve them, and the benchmark evidence about Israeli media habits does not describe them either — both gaps are real and neither is closed by more Hebrew research.
20	
21	**Trust in the institutions being tracked is itself low.** IDI's Democracy Index 2025 — its 23rd — found trust in state institutions near record lows for a second year, with trust in the government at 25% among Jewish respondents and 17.5% among Arab respondents, though the general mood improved sharply (34% called the country's situation bad or very bad, down from 54%) ([IDI, Israeli Democracy Index 2025, selected findings](https://en.idi.org.il/publications/62717); [Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ahead-of-election-year-survey-finds-israelis-trust-in-democracy-remains-low/)). Separately, fewer than half the public expressed trust in the prime minister ([IDI, 40% overall](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/59940)). A statements corpus is a low-trust-environment product: the audience's default is suspicion of the figure *and* of whoever is reporting on the figure, which argues for showing sources over asserting verdicts.
22	
23	**Journalists here are under pressure, not just under-resourced.** The US section's story is contraction. Israel's adds coercion: RSF's 2025 index placed Israel 112th of 180, down from 101st, and RSF documents a year of pressure, intimidation and censorship of Israeli journalists ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/pressure-intimidation-and-censorship-israeli-journalists-have-faced-growing-repression-past-year)); CPJ reported in December 2025 on stepped-up censorship and suppression of independent reporting ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/2025/12/under-the-radar-israel-steps-up-censorship-and-suppression-of-independent-reporting/)); in November 2024 the cabinet voted to end all government advertising in and subscriptions to *Haaretz* ([Courthouse News](https://www.courthousenews.com/chilling-effect-israel-reforms-raise-press-freedom-fears/)). (These figures come from search-result reporting; rsf.org's own index and country pages returned HTTP 403 to this environment.) The practical implication for a tool: a journalist who will be attacked for a claim needs the receipt more than the verdict — the evidence trail that the CHI 2025 study found fact-checkers demand is not a nicety here.
24	
25	**Professionally, the fact-checking "segment" is one desk.** HaMashrokit at *Globes* is Israel's only IFCN-accredited fact-checker (see the competitor wiki). Where the US segment is hundreds of organisations competing for the same funders, the Israeli one is a handful of people — so the realistic relationship is supply, not substitution: a corpus that makes their monitoring step cheaper.
26	
27	**Researchers here are unusually well supplied — with parliamentary text.** The post-Twitter data vacuum the US section describes is real in Israel too for social and broadcast speech, but the parliamentary half is solved: the Knesset Corpus covers 1992–2024, 30M+ sentences, annotated and distributed through CLARIN's ParlaMint ([Language Resources and Evaluation](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10579-025-09833-4)), and Hebrew-specific models are trained on exactly it ([Knesset-DictaBERT](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20581)). Israeli academic demand is therefore likelier to be for what the corpus *lacks* — studio interviews, rallies, party channels — than for the chamber record.
28	
29	**Campaign and advocacy staff have a date.** The election is 27 October 2026 ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/judge-sets-date-for-next-scheduled-elections-for-october-2026/)). Whether Israeli party apparatuses or campaign consultancies buy statement archives — and from whom — was not established this pass and is an open question below; the American Bridge-scale opposition-research industry described in the US section has no confirmed Israeli equivalent.
30	
31	## General public / engaged citizens (US research, as background)
32	
33	**Trust in fact-checkers is deeply partisan.** Pew found 70% of Republicans say fact-checkers "tend to favor one side" vs 29% of Democrats — a 41-point gap; overall Americans split roughly 50/48 on whether fact-checkers deal fairly ([Pew Research, 2019](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/06/27/republicans-far-more-likely-than-democrats-to-say-fact-checkers-tend-to-favor-one-side/)). The academic literature confirms the audience skew: awareness, positive attitudes and self-reported use of fact-checking sites concentrate among liberals, mainstream-news consumers, and the more educated ([Robertson, Mourão & Thorson 2020, International Journal of Press/Politics](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1940161219898055)); Republicans are more skeptical of all fact-check label types ([HKS Misinformation Review](https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/article/journalistic-interventions-matter-understanding-how-americans-perceive-fact-checking-labels/)). Implication for a browse-anyone tool: neutrality of method does not buy a neutral audience.
34	
35	**The backfire effect is largely debunked — corrections work.** Wood and Porter's replication attempts (5 experiments, 10,000+ participants, 52 issues) found no items triggering backfire ([ScienceDirect review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211368120300516)); Nyhan and co-authors now argue durability of misperceptions is not explained by backfire ([PNAS 2020](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1912440117)); Full Fact's own review reached the same conclusion ([Full Fact report, PDF](https://fullfact.org/media/uploads/backfire_report_fullfact.pdf)). Subjects even accept corrections of allied politicians, though belief improvements are modest.
36	
37	**Demand is event-driven and spiky, not steady.** Google searches for "fact check" spiked +650% during a November 2019 Democratic debate ([The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/471437-heres-what-searches-spiked-on-google-in-response-to-democrats-debate/)), and a broad debate fact-check was among the top queries during a 2024 VP debate ([Washington Examiner](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/campaigns/presidential/3174106/what-people-were-searching-vp-debate/)). The same pattern shows on Wikipedia: candidate pageviews surge just before elections and correlate with outcomes ([EPJ Data Science](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjds/s13688-016-0083-3); [Washington Post on the mechanism](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/politics/2016-election/presidential-wikipedias/)), with Nikki Haley's page reportedly reaching ~450K views/day around the 2024 early contests (traffic figures per search-result coverage; not independently verified). Baseline fact-check site traffic is modest between events — per Ahrefs, PolitiFact saw ~122K visits in May 2025 vs Snopes ~252K ([Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com/websites/politifact.com/competitors); analytics-vendor estimate, not publisher-reported). Reuters Institute's 2025 report adds that when people verify suspicious content they go first to trusted news brands, but increasingly also to AI chatbots and social media — a "flatter" verification hierarchy ([DNR 2025 executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025/dnr-executive-summary)); 58% globally worry about telling real from fake news, 73% in the US ([full PDF](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2025-06/Digital_News-Report_2025.pdf)).
38	
39	## Journalists and fact-checkers
40	
41	**The claim-finding step is already partially automated — by the fact-checking community itself.** Duke Reporters' Lab's Tech & Check runs ClaimBuster over transcripts and social posts and emails fact-checkers daily lists of checkable statements; its Fact-Check Insights database holds structured data on 180,000+ checked claims via the ClaimReview schema ([Duke Sanford](https://sanford.duke.edu/blog-post/duke-reporters-lab-gives-fact-checkers-researchers-new-tools-thwart-misinformation/)). This is the strongest signal of what the bottleneck is: finding and re-finding what a figure said, at scale, across sources.
42	
43	**Their current tool stack is fragmented and expensive.** Broadcast monitoring runs through TVEyes (2.5M+ hours of broadcast/month, real-time transcripts and alerts — [TVEyes](https://www.tveyes.com/)) and clip marketplaces like Grabien, which monitors live events and sells professionally cut, transcribed clips ([Grabien](https://grabien.com/)). Print archive search means Nexis, historically ~$600/month per seat — a freelancer-negotiated group deal at $26/month was newsworthy in itself ([Tools for Reporters](https://toolsforreporters.com/2021/03/24/a-nexis-for-the-rest-of-us/)). Transcription is commodity, with the key journalist feature being timestamp-linked audio for quote verification ([The Media Copilot](https://mediacopilot.ai/the-best-ai-transcription-tools-for-journalists-hands-on-review/)). C-SPAN's archive — 200,000+ hours since 1987, word-level searchable — is the free gold standard but covers only official proceedings and its own programming ([Purdue researcher guide, PDF](https://cla.purdue.edu/communication/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/How-To-Guide-for-Researchers-C-SPAN-Archives.pdf)).
44	
45	**The people doing this work are disappearing.** 270,000+ US newspaper jobs gone since 2005 (75%+); 1,200 newspaper and 1,800 digital-publisher journalist jobs lost in the past year alone ([Medill State of Local News 2025](https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/2025/report/); [Nieman Lab](https://www.niemanlab.org/2025/10/in-medills-latest-state-of-local-news-report-a-festering-20-year-old-problem-looms-larger-than-ever/)). Full-time newspaper statehouse reporters fell from 374 (2014) to 245 (2022) ([Pew media layoffs topic page](https://www.pewresearch.org/topic/news-habits-media/news-media-trends/media-industry/media-layoffs-employment/)). Fact-checking itself is contracting: Duke's census counted 443 active projects in 2025, down from 451, with ~30 closures vs 10 launches, as Meta ended its US third-party program ([Duke census — reporterslab.org is egress-blocked from this environment; figures per search results attributing them to the Duke Reporters' Lab censuses](https://reporterslab.org/2025/06/19/fact-checkers-persevere-as-politicians-platforms-turn-up-heat/); see also [Poynter on the 2026 census](https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/2026/fact-checking-projects-survive-funding-cuts-duke-census/)). IFCN's State of the Fact-Checkers surveys report 76% of organizations describing finances as vulnerable or in crisis even while 62% grew audiences, and ~72% facing harassment ([Rappler on the 2025 report](https://www.rappler.com/world/global-affairs/state-fact-checkers-report-2025-ifcn/); [Poynter on the 2023 report](https://www.poynter.org/ifcn/2024/state-fact-checkers-report-2023-findings/)). A CHI 2025 study documents fact-checkers' explicit requirement that any automated assistance show its evidence trail — opaque verdicts are unusable to them ([ACM CHI 2025](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713277)).
46	
47	## Researchers and academics
48	
49	**Today's corpora are institution-centric, not person-centric.** The workhorses: UCSB's American Presidency Project (163,161 records as of 2024, presidents 1789–present, run by two academics since 1999 — [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_American_Presidency_Project); [APP about page](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/about)); ParlSpeech V2 (6.3M parliamentary speeches, 9 democracies, harmonized metadata, on Harvard Dataverse — [Dataverse](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/L4OAKN)); UK Hansard scraped from official HTML. All cover formal settings (chamber floor, official documents); interviews, rallies, podcasts and TV hits — where contradictions actually surface — are largely uncorpused.
50	
51	**The Twitter API shutdown left a documented data vacuum.** Free academic access ended early 2023; the replacement enterprise tier started at $42,000/month, halting 100+ active projects and 250+ planned ones and pushing doctoral students to change topics ([Fast Company](https://www.fastcompany.com/91040397/under-elon-musk-x-is-denying-api-access-to-academics-who-study-misinformation); [Coalition for Independent Technology Research letter](https://independenttechresearch.org/letter-twitters-new-api-plans-will-devastate-public-interest-research/); ["RIP Twitter API" eulogy, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07340)). There is still no academic tier in 2026 ([xcrop.io overview](https://xcrop.io/blog/twitter-data-academic-research)). A stable, exportable statements corpus lands directly in this gap.
52	
53	**The substitute researchers actually adopted is broadcast, not social.** Where the text corpora went dark, the Internet Archive's TV News Archive stayed free and grew: closed captions indexed across 9.5 million broadcasts and 6.6 million hours from 108 channels in 50 countries and 35 languages over 20 years, with GDELT's Visual Explorer rendering each broadcast as a thumbnail grid and letting the thumbnails be downloaded in bulk for non-consumptive computational analysis ([GDELT: Visual Explorer](https://blog.gdeltproject.org/visual-explorer-unlocking-9-5-million-broadcasts-6-6-million-hours-of-television-news/)). GDELT reports 2,000+ articles and research papers drawing on the holdings over the archive's first decade ([GDELT: the TV News Archive turns 10](https://blog.gdeltproject.org/the-internet-archives-tv-news-archive-turns-10-a-look-back-at-a-decade-of-pioneering-collaboration-reimagining-media-research/)), and web-science groups have published tooling for treating it as research data ([WS-DL: Tools for Using the Internet Archive's TV News Archive as Research Data](https://ws-dl.blogspot.com/2024/08/2024-08-07-tools-for-using-internet.html)). The asymmetry is the useful part: what a figure said *on camera* is well-corpused and free; what they said in text and on social platforms is the starved half — which is where hitbut's gap actually sits.
54	
55	**Replication norms make stable identifiers and dumps a hard requirement, not a nicety.** AJPS has required open replication data since 2012; sharing rose from ~8% of political-science articles in 2012 to 31% in 2022 — meaning 69% still don't, partly because sources are hard to package ([PS: Political Science & Politics](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/data-and-code-availability-in-political-science-publications-from-1995-to-2022/F95EA30BEDC1B7A52CAE143D332B0746); [AJPS guidelines, PDF](https://ajps.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/ajps_replication-guidelines-2-1.pdf)). Harvard Dataverse is the de facto deposit venue. Separately, stance detection over political text is an active NLP subfield with its own datasets (P-STANCE, SemEval-2016), but tracking one figure's position *changes over time* is noted as under-served ([LLM stance-detection survey, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.08464); [Cambridge PSRM practical guide](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-science-research-and-methods/article/stance-detection-a-practical-guide-to-classifying-political-beliefs-in-text/E227E746BD7D9751526DA0EC2C378787)) — hitbut's contradiction layer is itself a publishable dataset.
56	
57	## Campaign and advocacy staff
58	
59	**"Tracking" is a physical, industrial practice with real budgets.** American Bridge (D) grew from 20 trackers in 2012 to 44 trackers in 41 states on ~$18M/year; America Rising (R) ran ~$8M/year with 27 full-time trackers in 24 states — twenty-somethings filming targets' every public utterance, with footage analyzed and archived at DC-area headquarters ([Yahoo/HuffPost](https://news.yahoo.com/down-candidate-era-nothing-matters-201024378.html); [Slate on America Rising](https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2014/01/america-rising-the-republican-pac-that-s-filming-every-vulnerable-democratic-candidate.html); [PBS Frontline on the rise of the "campaign stalker" post-Citizens United](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/frontline/article/citizens-united-and-the-rise-of-the-campaign-stalker/)). America Rising even monetized its archive by selling candidate photos and research to paying clients ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/america-rising-trackers-to-sell-candidate-photos-at-a-competitive-price)).
60	
61	**Oppo research is bought per-book, at prices that make an automated corpus look free.** A local/statewide oppo book runs $10,000–$50,000; one firm publicly prices a "Core Book" at $19,375–$23,250 depending on turnaround ([Nesbitt & Parrinello pricing page](https://www.nesbittresearch.com/opposition-research-price/)). Candidates also commission "self-research" books to know their own vulnerabilities ([The Campaign Workshop](https://www.thecampaignworkshop.com/blog/advocacy-campaigns/opposition-research)). The war-room workflow this feeds — rapid response, clip cutting, flip-flop hunting — is serviced today by Grabien's TVClipper and live-event monitoring ([Grabien TVClipper](https://grabien.com/tvclipper)).
62	
63	**Media monitoring is a multi-billion-dollar spend category.** 2025 market-size estimates from research firms cluster at $5.4–6.3B globally, ~11–12% CAGR, North America ~37% of it ([Mordor Intelligence](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/media-monitoring-market); [Fortune Business Insights](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/media-monitoring-tools-market-104157); vendor market-research estimates — origins differ, treat as a range).
64	
65	## Cross-cutting
66	
67	- **The precedent product is editorial, not computational.** PolitiFact's Flip-O-Meter (launched 2008: No Flip / Half Flip / Full Flop) is exactly hitbut's consistency use case, done by hand per-claim, explicitly framed as informational rather than judgmental ([PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/article/2008/aug/05/introducing-flip-o-meter/)). It has no corpus, no API, no alerts.
68	- **Supply-demand scissors.** Verification demand spikes around events while paid human capacity (newsrooms, fact-check orgs, oppo shops) shrinks or stays boutique — the structural opening for an automated, citable corpus serving all four segments from one backend.
69	- **Show-the-work is the universal requirement.** Fact-checkers demand evidence trails from automation ([CHI 2025](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713277)), academics demand replication files, and public-trust research says the partisan audience gap is the main adoption risk — per-statement sourcing is the one feature every segment names.
70

144	- How many working journalists are there in Israel, and what has the trend been since 2023? English-language searches returned only global layoff data; this needs Hebrew industry sources (Union of Journalists, the Seventh Eye).

146	- Do Israeli researchers use the Knesset Corpus in practice, and what do they say is missing from it? Uptake was not measured this pass.
147	- Election-period demand: is there Israeli search-interest or traffic evidence for fact-checking spikes around a campaign, comparable to the US debate spikes?

149	## Growth log

Header rewritten Israel-first, keeping only the backfire-effect finding from the US set as genuinely transferable.
152	- **2026-08-23** — Partly answered the post-2023 academic-substitutes question: the Internet Archive TV News Archive plus GDELT's explorers are the substitute with documented uptake (9.5M broadcasts, 6.6M hours, 2,000+ papers over a decade), which splits the data vacuum in two — broadcast speech is well-corpused and free, text and social speech are not. Open question narrowed to the text half.
153	- **2026-08-21** — Page seeded (initial research scan, deferred at adoption): researched all four segments — public trust and demand patterns, journalist/fact-checker workflows and contraction, academic corpora and the post-Twitter data vacuum, and the opposition-research industry's practices and budgets.

# User research — the four target segments

## Key insights

- Israel votes on 27 October 2026 — a fixed deadline, and the first Knesset to serve a full term since 1988
- Trust in Israeli media averages 46% and splits by channel, from Kan 11 at 60% down to Channel 14 at 35%
- 52% of Israelis get news through WhatsApp or Telegram — messaging is a primary news channel, not a side one
- The benchmark Israeli media survey covers only the Jewish public; the 2.1M Arab citizens were not measured
- Israel's professional fact-checking segment is one newsroom desk, so the field is a supplier, not a rival
- Israel fell to 112th in RSF's 2025 press-freedom index from 101st, and the cabinet cut off Haaretz's state ads
- Backfire effect failed to replicate: 10,000+ subjects, 52 issues, zero backfires — corrections do move beliefs

## Who these segments actually are in Israel

The four segments below were researched against the US and are kept as transferable background on how people respond to corrections and what practitioners need. This section is the Israeli reading of the same four, and it is where the sizes and the habits come from.

**The public: online, messaged, and only half-trusting.** The Israel Democracy Institute's media survey (published 26 May 2024, led by Tehilla Shwartz Altshuler and Inna Orly Sapozhnikova) found 63% of respondents check news online daily, 59.5% use social media for news, 58% rely on television, **52% get news through WhatsApp or Telegram**, 36% radio and 16% print. Average trust in the media stood at 46%, split hard by outlet: Kan 11 at 60%, Channel 12 at 54%, Channel 13 at 46%, Channel 14 at 35%. 56% believe they can distinguish fake news from factual reporting, and about 70% believe they can separate news from commentary ([IDI: Media and Social Media Consumption, Trust, and Literacy](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/54235)). Two things follow. Messaging apps are a first-class news channel here in a way they are not in the US data above, so a shareable per-statement link matters more than a destination site. And the trust split runs by *channel*, not only by party — which is the Israeli form of the partisan-audience problem the US section describes.

**A fifth of the country is outside the survey and outside the language.** The IDI survey covered the Jewish population only; a companion survey of Arab citizens' habits was planned separately. Arab citizens are 2.147 million people, 21.1% of the population ([CBS figures as reported](https://israel.com/public/israel-starts-2026-with-more-than-10-million-people/)). A Hebrew-only product does not serve them, and the benchmark evidence about Israeli media habits does not describe them either — both gaps are real and neither is closed by more Hebrew research.

**Trust in the institutions being tracked is itself low.** IDI's Democracy Index 2025 — its 23rd — found trust in state institutions near record lows for a second year, with trust in the government at 25% among Jewish respondents and 17.5% among Arab respondents, though the general mood improved sharply (34% called the country's situation bad or very bad, down from 54%) ([IDI, Israeli Democracy Index 2025, selected findings](https://en.idi.org.il/publications/62717); [Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ahead-of-election-year-survey-finds-israelis-trust-in-democracy-remains-low/)). Separately, fewer than half the public expressed trust in the prime minister ([IDI, 40% overall](https://en.idi.org.il/articles/59940)). A statements corpus is a low-trust-environment product: the audience's default is suspicion of the figure *and* of whoever is reporting on the figure, which argues for showing sources over asserting verdicts.

**Journalists here are under pressure, not just under-resourced.** The US section's story is contraction. Israel's adds coercion: RSF's 2025 index placed Israel 112th of 180, down from 101st, and RSF documents a year of pressure, intimidation and censorship of Israeli journalists ([RSF](https://rsf.org/en/pressure-intimidation-and-censorship-israeli-journalists-have-faced-growing-repression-past-year)); CPJ reported in December 2025 on stepped-up censorship and suppression of independent reporting ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/2025/12/under-the-radar-israel-steps-up-censorship-and-suppression-of-independent-reporting/)); in November 2024 the cabinet voted to end all government advertising in and subscriptions to *Haaretz* ([Courthouse News](https://www.courthousenews.com/chilling-effect-israel-reforms-raise-press-freedom-fears/)). (These figures come from search-result reporting; rsf.org's own index and country pages returned HTTP 403 to this environment.) The practical implication for a tool: a journalist who will be attacked for a claim needs the receipt more than the verdict — the evidence trail that the CHI 2025 study found fact-checkers demand is not a nicety here.

**Professionally, the fact-checking "segment" is one desk.** HaMashrokit at *Globes* is Israel's only IFCN-accredited fact-checker (see the competitor wiki). Where the US segment is hundreds of organisations competing for the same funders, the Israeli one is a handful of people — so the realistic relationship is supply, not substitution: a corpus that makes their monitoring step cheaper.

**Researchers here are unusually well supplied — with parliamentary text.** The post-Twitter data vacuum the US section describes is real in Israel too for social and broadcast speech, but the parliamentary half is solved: the Knesset Corpus covers 1992–2024, 30M+ sentences, annotated and distributed through CLARIN's ParlaMint ([Language Resources and Evaluation](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10579-025-09833-4)), and Hebrew-specific models are trained on exactly it ([Knesset-DictaBERT](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20581)). Israeli academic demand is therefore likelier to be for what the corpus *lacks* — studio interviews, rallies, party channels — than for the chamber record.

**Campaign and advocacy staff have a date.** The election is 27 October 2026 ([Times of Israel](https://www.timesofisrael.com/judge-sets-date-for-next-scheduled-elections-for-october-2026/)). Whether Israeli party apparatuses or campaign consultancies buy statement archives — and from whom — was not established this pass and is an open question below; the American Bridge-scale opposition-research industry described in the US section has no confirmed Israeli equivalent.

## General public / engaged citizens (US research, as background)

**Trust in fact-checkers is deeply partisan.** Pew found 70% of Republicans say fact-checkers "tend to favor one side" vs 29% of Democrats — a 41-point gap; overall Americans split roughly 50/48 on whether fact-checkers deal fairly ([Pew Research, 2019](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2019/06/27/republicans-far-more-likely-than-democrats-to-say-fact-checkers-tend-to-favor-one-side/)). The academic literature confirms the audience skew: awareness, positive attitudes and self-reported use of fact-checking sites concentrate among liberals, mainstream-news consumers, and the more educated ([Robertson, Mourão & Thorson 2020, International Journal of Press/Politics](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1940161219898055)); Republicans are more skeptical of all fact-check label types ([HKS Misinformation Review](https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/article/journalistic-interventions-matter-understanding-how-americans-perceive-fact-checking-labels/)). Implication for a browse-anyone tool: neutrality of method does not buy a neutral audience.

**The backfire effect is largely debunked — corrections work.** Wood and Porter's replication attempts (5 experiments, 10,000+ participants, 52 issues) found no items triggering backfire ([ScienceDirect review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2211368120300516)); Nyhan and co-authors now argue durability of misperceptions is not explained by backfire ([PNAS 2020](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1912440117)); Full Fact's own review reached the same conclusion ([Full Fact report, PDF](https://fullfact.org/media/uploads/backfire_report_fullfact.pdf)). Subjects even accept corrections of allied politicians, though belief improvements are modest.

**Demand is event-driven and spiky, not steady.** Google searches for "fact check" spiked +650% during a November 2019 Democratic debate ([The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/471437-heres-what-searches-spiked-on-google-in-response-to-democrats-debate/)), and a broad debate fact-check was among the top queries during a 2024 VP debate ([Washington Examiner](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/campaigns/presidential/3174106/what-people-were-searching-vp-debate/)). The same pattern shows on Wikipedia: candidate pageviews surge just before elections and correlate with outcomes ([EPJ Data Science](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjds/s13688-016-0083-3); [Washington Post on the mechanism](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/politics/2016-election/presidential-wikipedias/)), with Nikki Haley's page reportedly reaching ~450K views/day around the 2024 early contests (traffic figures per search-result coverage; not independently verified). Baseline fact-check site traffic is modest between events — per Ahrefs, PolitiFact saw ~122K visits in May 2025 vs Snopes ~252K ([Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com/websites/politifact.com/competitors); analytics-vendor estimate, not publisher-reported). Reuters Institute's 2025 report adds that when people verify suspicious content they go first to trusted news brands, but increasingly also to AI chatbots and social media — a "flatter" verification hierarchy ([DNR 2025 executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2025/dnr-executive-summary)); 58% globally worry about telling real from fake news, 73% in the US ([full PDF](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2025-06/Digital_News-Report_2025.pdf)).

## Journalists and fact-checkers

**The claim-finding step is already partially automated — by the fact-checking community itself.** Duke Reporters' Lab's Tech & Check runs ClaimBuster over transcripts and social posts and emails fact-checkers daily lists of checkable statements; its Fact-Check Insights database holds structured data on 180,000+ checked claims via the ClaimReview schema ([Duke Sanford](https://sanford.duke.edu/blog-post/duke-reporters-lab-gives-fact-checkers-researchers-new-tools-thwart-misinformation/)). This is the strongest signal of what the bottleneck is: finding and re-finding what a figure said, at scale, across sources.

**Their current tool stack is fragmented and expensive.** Broadcast monitoring runs through TVEyes (2.5M+ hours of broadcast/month, real-time transcripts and alerts — [TVEyes](https://www.tveyes.com/)) and clip marketplaces like Grabien, which monitors live events and sells professionally cut, transcribed clips ([Grabien](https://grabien.com/)). Print archive search means Nexis, historically ~$600/month per seat — a freelancer-negotiated group deal at $26/month was newsworthy in itself ([Tools for Reporters](https://toolsforreporters.com/2021/03/24/a-nexis-for-the-rest-of-us/)). Transcription is commodity, with the key journalist feature being timestamp-linked audio for quote verification ([The Media Copilot](https://mediacopilot.ai/the-best-ai-transcription-tools-for-journalists-hands-on-review/)). C-SPAN's archive — 200,000+ hours since 1987, word-level searchable — is the free gold standard but covers only official proceedings and its own programming ([Purdue researcher guide, PDF](https://cla.purdue.edu/communication/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/How-To-Guide-for-Researchers-C-SPAN-Archives.pdf)).

**The people doing this work are disappearing.** 270,000+ US newspaper jobs gone since 2005 (75%+); 1,200 newspaper and 1,800 digital-publisher journalist jobs lost in the past year alone ([Medill State of Local News 2025](https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/2025/report/); [Nieman Lab](https://www.niemanlab.org/2025/10/in-medills-latest-state-of-local-news-report-a-festering-20-year-old-problem-looms-larger-than-ever/)). Full-time newspaper statehouse reporters fell from 374 (2014) to 245 (2022) ([Pew media layoffs topic page](https://www.pewresearch.org/topic/news-habits-media/news-media-trends/media-industry/media-layoffs-employment/)). Fact-checking itself is contracting: Duke's census counted 443 active projects in 2025, down from 451, with ~30 closures vs 10 launches, as Meta ended its US third-party program ([Duke census — reporterslab.org is egress-blocked from this environment; figures per search results attributing them to the Duke Reporters' Lab censuses](https://reporterslab.org/2025/06/19/fact-checkers-persevere-as-politicians-platforms-turn-up-heat/); see also [Poynter on the 2026 census](https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/2026/fact-checking-projects-survive-funding-cuts-duke-census/)). IFCN's State of the Fact-Checkers surveys report 76% of organizations describing finances as vulnerable or in crisis even while 62% grew audiences, and ~72% facing harassment ([Rappler on the 2025 report](https://www.rappler.com/world/global-affairs/state-fact-checkers-report-2025-ifcn/); [Poynter on the 2023 report](https://www.poynter.org/ifcn/2024/state-fact-checkers-report-2023-findings/)). A CHI 2025 study documents fact-checkers' explicit requirement that any automated assistance show its evidence trail — opaque verdicts are unusable to them ([ACM CHI 2025](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713277)).

## Researchers and academics

**Today's corpora are institution-centric, not person-centric.** The workhorses: UCSB's American Presidency Project (163,161 records as of 2024, presidents 1789–present, run by two academics since 1999 — [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_American_Presidency_Project); [APP about page](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/about)); ParlSpeech V2 (6.3M parliamentary speeches, 9 democracies, harmonized metadata, on Harvard Dataverse — [Dataverse](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/L4OAKN)); UK Hansard scraped from official HTML. All cover formal settings (chamber floor, official documents); interviews, rallies, podcasts and TV hits — where contradictions actually surface — are largely uncorpused.

**The Twitter API shutdown left a documented data vacuum.** Free academic access ended early 2023; the replacement enterprise tier started at $42,000/month, halting 100+ active projects and 250+ planned ones and pushing doctoral students to change topics ([Fast Company](https://www.fastcompany.com/91040397/under-elon-musk-x-is-denying-api-access-to-academics-who-study-misinformation); [Coalition for Independent Technology Research letter](https://independenttechresearch.org/letter-twitters-new-api-plans-will-devastate-public-interest-research/); ["RIP Twitter API" eulogy, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07340)). There is still no academic tier in 2026 ([xcrop.io overview](https://xcrop.io/blog/twitter-data-academic-research)). A stable, exportable statements corpus lands directly in this gap.

**The substitute researchers actually adopted is broadcast, not social.** Where the text corpora went dark, the Internet Archive's TV News Archive stayed free and grew: closed captions indexed across 9.5 million broadcasts and 6.6 million hours from 108 channels in 50 countries and 35 languages over 20 years, with GDELT's Visual Explorer rendering each broadcast as a thumbnail grid and letting the thumbnails be downloaded in bulk for non-consumptive computational analysis ([GDELT: Visual Explorer](https://blog.gdeltproject.org/visual-explorer-unlocking-9-5-million-broadcasts-6-6-million-hours-of-television-news/)). GDELT reports 2,000+ articles and research papers drawing on the holdings over the archive's first decade ([GDELT: the TV News Archive turns 10](https://blog.gdeltproject.org/the-internet-archives-tv-news-archive-turns-10-a-look-back-at-a-decade-of-pioneering-collaboration-reimagining-media-research/)), and web-science groups have published tooling for treating it as research data ([WS-DL: Tools for Using the Internet Archive's TV News Archive as Research Data](https://ws-dl.blogspot.com/2024/08/2024-08-07-tools-for-using-internet.html)). The asymmetry is the useful part: what a figure said *on camera* is well-corpused and free; what they said in text and on social platforms is the starved half — which is where hitbut's gap actually sits.

**Replication norms make stable identifiers and dumps a hard requirement, not a nicety.** AJPS has required open replication data since 2012; sharing rose from ~8% of political-science articles in 2012 to 31% in 2022 — meaning 69% still don't, partly because sources are hard to package ([PS: Political Science & Politics](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/data-and-code-availability-in-political-science-publications-from-1995-to-2022/F95EA30BEDC1B7A52CAE143D332B0746); [AJPS guidelines, PDF](https://ajps.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/ajps_replication-guidelines-2-1.pdf)). Harvard Dataverse is the de facto deposit venue. Separately, stance detection over political text is an active NLP subfield with its own datasets (P-STANCE, SemEval-2016), but tracking one figure's position *changes over time* is noted as under-served ([LLM stance-detection survey, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.08464); [Cambridge PSRM practical guide](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-science-research-and-methods/article/stance-detection-a-practical-guide-to-classifying-political-beliefs-in-text/E227E746BD7D9751526DA0EC2C378787)) — hitbut's contradiction layer is itself a publishable dataset.

## Campaign and advocacy staff

**"Tracking" is a physical, industrial practice with real budgets.** American Bridge (D) grew from 20 trackers in 2012 to 44 trackers in 41 states on ~$18M/year; America Rising (R) ran ~$8M/year with 27 full-time trackers in 24 states — twenty-somethings filming targets' every public utterance, with footage analyzed and archived at DC-area headquarters ([Yahoo/HuffPost](https://news.yahoo.com/down-candidate-era-nothing-matters-201024378.html); [Slate on America Rising](https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2014/01/america-rising-the-republican-pac-that-s-filming-every-vulnerable-democratic-candidate.html); [PBS Frontline on the rise of the "campaign stalker" post-Citizens United](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/frontline/article/citizens-united-and-the-rise-of-the-campaign-stalker/)). America Rising even monetized its archive by selling candidate photos and research to paying clients ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/america-rising-trackers-to-sell-candidate-photos-at-a-competitive-price)).

**Oppo research is bought per-book, at prices that make an automated corpus look free.** A local/statewide oppo book runs $10,000–$50,000; one firm publicly prices a "Core Book" at $19,375–$23,250 depending on turnaround ([Nesbitt & Parrinello pricing page](https://www.nesbittresearch.com/opposition-research-price/)). Candidates also commission "self-research" books to know their own vulnerabilities ([The Campaign Workshop](https://www.thecampaignworkshop.com/blog/advocacy-campaigns/opposition-research)). The war-room workflow this feeds — rapid response, clip cutting, flip-flop hunting — is serviced today by Grabien's TVClipper and live-event monitoring ([Grabien TVClipper](https://grabien.com/tvclipper)).

**Media monitoring is a multi-billion-dollar spend category.** 2025 market-size estimates from research firms cluster at $5.4–6.3B globally, ~11–12% CAGR, North America ~37% of it ([Mordor Intelligence](https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/media-monitoring-market); [Fortune Business Insights](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/media-monitoring-tools-market-104157); vendor market-research estimates — origins differ, treat as a range).

## Cross-cutting

- **The precedent product is editorial, not computational.** PolitiFact's Flip-O-Meter (launched 2008: No Flip / Half Flip / Full Flop) is exactly hitbut's consistency use case, done by hand per-claim, explicitly framed as informational rather than judgmental ([PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/article/2008/aug/05/introducing-flip-o-meter/)). It has no corpus, no API, no alerts.
- **Supply-demand scissors.** Verification demand spikes around events while paid human capacity (newsrooms, fact-check orgs, oppo shops) shrinks or stays boutique — the structural opening for an automated, citable corpus serving all four segments from one backend.
- **Show-the-work is the universal requirement.** Fact-checkers demand evidence trails from automation ([CHI 2025](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706598.3713277)), academics demand replication files, and public-trust research says the partisan audience gap is the main adoption risk — per-statement sourcing is the one feature every segment names.

- Does the IDI companion survey of Arab citizens' media habits exist yet, and what does it say? A fifth of the country is unmeasured in the benchmark used here.
- Is there Israeli evidence on the partisan-trust gap in fact-checkers, equivalent to Pew's 70/29 US split — and does it attach to primary-source archives as well as to verdicts?
- Do Israeli campaigns, party apparatuses or consultancies buy statement archives or opposition research today, and from whom? No Israeli equivalent of American Bridge was found.

# Fetching from the web

- **Needing exact text** — a summarizing fetch tool is not a source; when the bytes matter, `curl`
  into the scratchpad and read from disk.
- **A `403`** — don't retry and don't try a sibling URL; attribute the search snippet to the
  publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it for re-verification.
- **A sandbox or proxy denial is a policy boundary, not an obstacle to route around** — no
  open-network runner, no ad-hoc CI workflow, no push-triggered probe to make the request from
  somewhere the policy does not apply. Answer from committed reference material or ask the owner,
  and say plainly that anything unverifiable is unverified.
- **An explicit egress block** (`EGRESS_BLOCKED`) is domain-wide, unlike a publisher's `403`:
  working down alternate sources for the same fact spends the same denial on each. Never file the
  gap as "re-verify next pass" — no later agent pass can cross a policy block either; mark it as
  needing a human or an unblocked environment.

## History of the Partnership

HaMashrokit (The Whistle) of Globes participated in Facebook's fact-checking program from April 2019 until early December 2020, working alongside dozens of other fact-checking organizations worldwide that are members of the IFCN network to identify and reduce exposure to false information on Facebook.

## Why the Partnership Ended in 2020

Concerns arose that fact-checking could create conflicts of interest and provide unfair competitive advantages to Globes, which could harm trust and contradict the values Globes set for itself, leading the Globes management to decide to discontinue HaMashrokit's participation in Facebook's program.

## Meta's Broader Fact-Checking Program Shutdown in 2025

More recently, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced that it would discontinue the fact-checking mechanism on Facebook and Instagram and replace it with a "community notes" system similar to X (formerly Twitter). This announcement came in January 2025, ending Meta's global fact-checking program entirely.

# Writing product-wiki pages

The rules a wiki page is held to while it is being edited. Which page to grow and where the
material comes from is the caller's business — the weekly
[wiki-growth](../../tasks/wiki-growth/task.md) pass picks from each page's open questions, and
[explore-link](../explore-link/SKILL.md) is handed a source — and both write under these.

- **Opening a page with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying
  the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the
  thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header
  understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing
  and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.

- **Writing an insight bullet.** One short line, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no
  citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would
  *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number
  nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely
  hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. A borderline-obvious line costs
  the reader two seconds; a long, careful line costs them the header.

- **Touching the header after a pass.** It is a current view, not a log. A pass that changes
  what a page's most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded insight
  leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below), and an insight the pass
  didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's top-line understanding, the header
  doesn't move.

- **Starting a pass on a page.** Compile once, refine in place: read the target page end to end
  before researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as open, thin,
  or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass. Never re-derive a claim that's
  already cited and current.

- **Writing a claim.** Cited, never silently rewritten: an uncited claim doesn't get written. A
  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted
  without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's growth log and updates the open
  questions in both directions.

- **Attributing a figure you saw in several places.** Recurrence is not evidence of who
  published it: search snippets quote each other, so a number that recurs across five results
  is one source repeated, and the firm the snippets name is routinely not the firm that produced
  it. When you cannot open the report, attribute the figure to the publisher a source
  explicitly names as its **origin**; when sources disagree about that, say so on the page
  rather than picking one.

- **Finding nothing citable.** No fabricated growth: most passes find little or nothing; no new
  citable material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.

- **Adding to `product-wiki/sample-data/`, or a new wiki folder.** sample-data gains a file only
  when a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test asserts against
  belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/` outside the two reserved
  names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so create one only deliberately, seeded with
  its required sections; automation refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.

- **Touching `product-wiki/product-requirements/`.** The sink is human-reviewed only, and it
  never changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding that
  should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.

- **Landing the change.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR — researched claims
  entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. The owner phrase **"grow the
  product wiki"** runs the worker method in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR
  discipline.

lines: **knesset-ai.com — the closest live competitor, and nobody's name is on it.** [knesset-ai.com](https://knesset-ai.com/) describes itself as "one landing page for Knesset discussions, laws, votes, MK members and political undercurrents". It carries plenary and committee protocols from the last five years, every law passed in third reading, full voting maps, and **per-MK pages with ideological analysis, "surprising votes", and recent quotes from proceedings with links to the protocols the member's name appears in** — statement tracking from 2022-01-01 onward. Access appears free; no operating organisation, funder or team is identified on the page, and no pricing is stated. This is the single most important competitive finding of this pass: much of the corpus-plus-per-figure-browsing layer already exists in Hebrew. What could not be established is who runs it, whether it is maintained, how good the extraction is, and whether it does anything with contradictions — all open questions below.

-**HaMashrokit (המשרוקית) of *Globes* — the verdict layer, with no corpus behind it.** Israel's only IFCN-accredited fact-checker, a signatory since 2018, operating as an independent unit inside *Globes* since January 2019 after two years (2017–2018) as an NGO; 300+ published checks since the July 2017 launch, roughly one item a day ([IFCN listing](https://ifcncodeofprinciples.poynter.org/application/public/the-whistle/661a8b0fba7689d48142c10b), [New Israel Fund on the *Globes* move](https://nif.org/stories/human-rights-democracy/the-whistle-integrated-into-globes-newspaper/)). Its published method is a five-stage pipeline — monitoring of radio, TV and social media by listeners; an editorial decision on whether a statement is checkable and publicly relevant; research against official sources and experts; editorial review including a right of reply; then a collective score — on a five-category scale: correct, inaccurate, misleading, false, and "לשיקולכם" ("for your judgment") for claims too complex to rate ([Globes, about HaMashrokit](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001372882); the scale was reworked from ten categories to five in August 2025). Its [2025 year-in-review](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001530848) reports that 57% of checked statements came out false or misleading, only 7% true-and-newsworthy (which the desk calls too low), and about an eighth nuanced or context-dependent; it names its own coverage gaps candidly — Arab parties, which appear little in Hebrew media, ultra-Orthodox parties, which speak through religious outlets, and Benny Gantz's State Camp.

+**HaMashrokit (המשרוקית) of *Globes* — the verdict layer, with no corpus behind it.** Israel's only IFCN-accredited fact-checker, a signatory since 2018, operating as an independent unit inside *Globes* since January 2019 after two years (2017–2018) as an NGO; 300+ published checks since the July 2017 launch, roughly one item a day ([IFCN listing](https://ifcncodeofprinciples.poynter.org/application/public/the-whistle/661a8b0fba7689d48142c10b), [New Israel Fund on the *Globes* move](https://nif.org/stories/human-rights-democracy/the-whistle-integrated-into-globes-newspaper/)). Its published method is a five-stage pipeline — monitoring of radio, TV and social media by listeners; an editorial decision on whether a statement is checkable and publicly relevant; research against official sources and experts; editorial review including a right of reply; then a collective score — on a five-category scale: correct, inaccurate, misleading, false, and "לשיקולכם" ("for your judgment") for claims too complex to rate ([Globes, about HaMashrokit](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001372882); the scale was reworked from ten categories to five in August 2025). It was briefly a Meta third-party fact-checking partner too, but Globes pulled it out of Facebook's program in **December 2020**, after roughly a year and a half in it, once management judged that policing other advertisers' content on the platform put Globes in a conflict of interest and gave it an unfair competitive edge ([Globes: HaMashrokit exits Facebook's fact-checking program](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001351356), read via search snippet — globes.co.il is egress-blocked from this environment). That is over four years before Meta's global wind-down of third-party fact-checking in January 2025, so the wind-down cost HaMashrokit nothing it had not already given up voluntarily. Its [2025 year-in-review](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001530848) reports that 57% of checked statements came out false or misleading, only 7% true-and-newsworthy (which the desk calls too low), and about an eighth nuanced or context-dependent; it names its own coverage gaps candidly — Arab parties, which appear little in Hebrew media, ultra-Orthodox parties, which speak through religious outlets, and Benny Gantz's State Camp.

The relationship to this product is complementary rather than competitive, and the shape of the gap is precise: HaMashrokit selects a claim, adjudicates it and publishes a verdict. It does not maintain a browsable per-figure record of what a figure has said over time, and its monitoring step — people listening to radio and TV — is exactly the step a corpus makes cheap. Its coverage gaps are also a corpus's natural strength: a chamber-record corpus captures Arab and Haredi MKs speaking in the Knesset regardless of whether they appear on Hebrew television.

lines: **Full Fact** (UK) is the technology leader. It has [three main AI tools: claim detection, repeated-claim alerts, and live TV/radio transcription cross-referenced against its fact-check library](https://fullfact.org/blog/2025/feb/how-ai-can-help-fact-checkers/) — the alerts let it contact an MP who keeps repeating a debunked claim, which is functionally repeat-inconsistency detection. Its claim-matching system [runs ~10 million sentence comparisons daily](https://newsmachines.beehiiv.com/p/how-full-fact-scales-human-fact-checking-with-ai-1), and the tools are [used by 40+ fact-checking organizations in 30+ countries, including for US election coverage](https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/2025/the-uks-fact-checkers-are-sending-their-ai-to-help-americans-cover-elections/). What it doesn't do: publish a browsable per-figure statement history for the public.

-**AP Fact Check** — status **unverified**. AP [stopped fact-checking for Facebook at the end of 2018](https://techcrunch.com/2019/02/01/snopes-and-ap-leave-facebook-fact-checking-partnership/) and its [IFCN signatory application exists on Poynter](https://ifcncodeofprinciples.poynter.org/application/public/ap-fact-check/3E3B10E8-15FA-931D-E3DB-2DBEAA35527B), but this pass found no reliable source confirming or denying that AP shut its standalone fact-check vertical (Poynter.org is egress-blocked from this environment). Flagged in open questions.

+**AP Fact Check** is alive and active as of 2026 — a 2026 roundup of reliable fact-checking sites lists it alongside PolitiFact and FactCheck.org, crediting it with AP's institutional sourcing and global bureau network and describing an ongoing focus on viral misinformation, health claims, image verification and scientific consensus, and a credibility-research catalog separately carries it as a live project ([2026 factually-accurate-sites roundup — Trilinea](https://blog.trilinea.com/the-most-factually-accurate-news-sites-in-2026/); [AP Factcheck — Credibility Coalition CredCatalog](https://credibilitycoalition.org/credcatalog/project/ap-factcheck/); both read via search snippet, egress-blocked here). That is distinct from AP [stopping fact-checking specifically *for Facebook* at the end of 2018](https://techcrunch.com/2019/02/01/snopes-and-ap-leave-facebook-fact-checking-partnership/) — a narrower withdrawal from one distribution partner, not from AP's own vertical, which [has an IFCN signatory application on file](https://ifcncodeofprinciples.poynter.org/application/public/ap-fact-check/3E3B10E8-15FA-931D-E3DB-2DBEAA35527B) and keeps operating.

**Washington Post Fact Checker** — the [Trump claims database](https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/politics/trump-claims-database/) is the largest per-figure claim corpus ever built by a newsroom: [30,573 false or misleading claims over four years, archived on Jan 20, 2021](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/01/24/trumps-false-or-misleading-claims-total-30573-over-four-years/) and never restarted for the second term ([methodology retrospective](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/how-fact-checker-tracked-trump-claims/2021/01/23/ad04b69a-5c1d-11eb-a976-bad6431e03e2_story.html)). Glenn Kessler, its editor for ~15 years, [took a buyout and left July 31, 2025](https://washingtoncitypaper.com/article/768821/fact-checker-glenn-kessler-exits-washington-post-buyout/), [saying he's "not sure" the paper will replace the role](https://www.thewrap.com/washington-post-fact-checker-exits/) ([his own account](https://glennkessler.substack.com/p/why-i-left-the-washington-post)). Lesson: even the flagship per-figure database was a manual, single-figure, single-newsroom effort that died with staffing changes.

 **knesset-ai.com — the closest live competitor, and nobody's name is on it.** [knesset-ai.com](https://knesset-ai.com/) describes itself as "one landing page for Knesset discussions, laws, votes, MK members and political undercurrents". It carries plenary and committee protocols from the last five years, every law passed in third reading, full voting maps, and **per-MK pages with ideological analysis, "surprising votes", and recent quotes from proceedings with links to the protocols the member's name appears in** — statement tracking from 2022-01-01 onward. Access appears free; no operating organisation, funder or team is identified on the page, and no pricing is stated. This is the single most important competitive finding of this pass: much of the corpus-plus-per-figure-browsing layer already exists in Hebrew. What could not be established is who runs it, whether it is maintained, how good the extraction is, and whether it does anything with contradictions — all open questions below.
 
-**HaMashrokit (המשרוקית) of *Globes* — the verdict layer, with no corpus behind it.** Israel's only IFCN-accredited fact-checker, a signatory since 2018, operating as an independent unit inside *Globes* since January 2019 after two years (2017–2018) as an NGO; 300+ published checks since the July 2017 launch, roughly one item a day ([IFCN listing](https://ifcncodeofprinciples.poynter.org/application/public/the-whistle/661a8b0fba7689d48142c10b), [New Israel Fund on the *Globes* move](https://nif.org/stories/human-rights-democracy/the-whistle-integrated-into-globes-newspaper/)). Its published method is a five-stage pipeline — monitoring of radio, TV and social media by listeners; an editorial decision on whether a statement is checkable and publicly relevant; research against official sources and experts; editorial review including a right of reply; then a collective score — on a five-category scale: correct, inaccurate, misleading, false, and "לשיקולכם" ("for your judgment") for claims too complex to rate ([Globes, about HaMashrokit](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001372882); the scale was reworked from ten categories to five in August 2025). It was briefly a Meta third-party fact-checking partner too, but Globes pulled it out of Facebook's program in **December 2020**, after roughly a year and a half in it, once management judged that policing other advertisers' content on the platform put Globes in a conflict of interest and gave it an unfair competitive edge ([Globes: HaMashrokit exits Facebook's fact-checking program](https://www.globes.co.il/news/article.aspx?did=1001351356), read via search snippet — globes.co.il is egress-blocked from this environment). - **2026-08-21** — Page seeded (initial research scan, deferred at adoption): surveyed the fact-checking field's 2025 funding/distribution double shock, civic-tech sustainability record, commercial media-monitoring market, AI fact-checking automation, the manual status quo, and US legal terrain for scraping and verdict-style claims.

input.body:
## What was researched

Picked the two open questions most worth this run's judgment call: whether HaMashrokit was still a Meta/Facebook third-party fact-checking partner through Meta's 2025 global wind-down (asked in both `competitor-landscape` and `market-landscape`), and AP Fact Check's "status unverified" flag in `competitor-landscape`. Also attempted to advance the `competitor-landscape` page's top priority — who runs knesset-ai.com — and to re-verify the Knesset OData API claims flagged open in `market-landscape`.

## What changed, and where

- **`product-wiki/competitor-landscape/README.md`** — HaMashrokit paragraph: it *was* a Meta/Facebook program partner, but Globes pulled it out in December 2020 over a conflict-of-interest concern, over four years before Meta's 2025 wind-down — so the wind-down cost it nothing. AP Fact Check paragraph: rewritten from "status unverified" to confirmed alive and active as of 2026 (a 2026 fact-checking-sites roundup and a credibility-research catalog both list it as live); the earlier note had conflated AP's narrower 2018 exit from *Facebook's* program with its own vertical shutting down. Open question on the HaMashrokit/Meta relationship removed; growth log entry added.
- **`product-wiki/market-landscape/README.md`** — Same HaMashrokit/Meta finding added to its "one desk" paragraph; its open question removed. Annotated the two open questions about the Knesset OData API and committee-protocol structure with this pass's environment finding (see below); growth log entry added.

## Citations added

- Globes: "HaMashrokit exits Facebook's fact-checking program" (`did=1001351356`) — read via search snippet
- A 2026 factually-accurate-news-sites roundup (Trilinea) and the Credibility Coalition's CredCatalog AP Factcheck listing — both read via search snippet

## Environment note

Direct `WebFetch` to every domain tried this pass — globes.co.il, knesset-ai.com, knesset.gov.il, fs.knesset.gov.il, Wikipedia, archive.org — returned an egress block, where `knesset.gov.il`/`fs.knesset.gov.il` were reachable and verified first-hand as recently as the 2026-08-23 pass. `WebSearch` still worked, so this pass used the wiki's existing search-snippet citation convention throughout. This blocked any progress on the knesset-ai.com operator/maintenance question (the page's stated top priority) and on re-verifying the Knesset OData API claims — both stay open, the latter now noting the environment finding so a session with API access (or a human) can pick it up.

## Open questions left for the next run

- Who runs/maintains knesset-ai.com, and does it attempt contradiction detection? (unchanged — still the page's top priority, blocked this pass by egress)
- Does the Knesset OData service exclude per-MK voting and pre-18th-Knesset data, and are committee protocols structured like plenum ones? (needs direct API/file access)
- Everything else in each page's `## Open questions` is unchanged.

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.

   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
